Interactive “Message Wall”

A digital drawing wall for G-Dragon Media Exhibition: Übermensch IN OSAKA. Visitors doodle on their own devices, watch their drawing appear on an LED screen, and keep a branded copy as a digital souvenir. Every drawing is shared with the artist after the exhibition.

MESSAGE WALL

Context

During my internship at CreativeMUT, I worked on integrating technology into exhibition spaces and helping artists exhibit their work in cities across Asia and the United States.

One of the artists we worked with was G-Dragon, a Korean musician and artist who wanted to share his new art brand alongside his previous musical works. His exhibitions were designed to be interactive, using technology to build a more personal connection between visitors and his work.

In the first month of my internship, we helped ship and exhibit his works for G-Dragon Media Exhibition: Übermensch IN TOKYO. The following month, we began planning the next exhibition, G-Dragon Media Exhibition: Übermensch IN OSAKA.

Problem

We needed to differentiate our Osaka exhibition from the Tokyo exhibition

Japan is well connected by public transportation like the high-speed Shinkansen, and many fans from across the country had already visited the Tokyo exhibition. We needed to differentiate the Osaka exhibition enough that Tokyo visitors would return, and Osaka locals would feel they weren't getting a lesser version.

An additional constraint emerged mid-planning: an LED screen near the exhibition exit needed a purpose.

We were designing for a new audience

The main UI/UX challenge was localization. I was used to designing products in English, for users familiar with American UI/UX trends and conventions. This product needed to be intuitive for Japanese visitors, and for an international audience more familiar with Asian UX conventions.

The interface also had to follow the design guidelines set for the entire exhibition, at the request of the artist's agency, so that whatever we built felt like part of the exhibition rather than a separate product.

How might we create a new digital experience that makes visitors want to return for the next exhibition?

Process

I set three design principles

No app, no account

Intergenerational accessibility

Exhibition visitors span a wide age range, and this was a new launch, so the interface needed to be as intuitive as possible.

MESSAGE WALL

Brand cohesion

Anything we built would follow the exhibition's design guidelines, so its visuals matched the rest of the exhibition.

320 390 430

Device consistency

Every visitor needed a stable, consistent experience, so we designed to reduce issues caused by different mobile devices and browsers.

I researched how visitors felt about the Tokyo exhibition

The Tokyo exhibition gained a lot of attention in Japan, so I used social media to understand visitors' impressions and pain points, and how a new experience could address them.

  • Visitors wanted to interact with the artist, even if indirectly.
  • Visitors valued the exhibition's freebies and souvenirs, expressing that they were useful for taking fun photos throughout the exhibition.
  • Japanese visitors shared their visits more actively on social media, compared to visitors in other cities.

The findings shaped what our design goals would be, and how we would work within the design principles we set for this project.

I proposed the idea in a timed brainstorm

The Message Wall started in a timed brainstorming session, where the team wrote down as many ideas as possible without stopping until time ran out. One of my ideas was a digital Doodle Board. After the session, the team raised constraints, and each of my responses changed the idea.

Team
Me
Digital Doodle BoardMESSAGE WALL

We learned from previous engagement walls

Once the idea was approved, I looked more closely at earlier engagement walls to see where we could improve the visitor experience.

Seoul installed iPads for digital submissions, but visitors couldn't save their work. Visitors left with nothing to keep.

Hong Kong used a physical message wall, but it created no lasting connection between visitors and the artist. Messages never reached the artist.

Osaka had to do both. Visitors should leave with something they made, and their messages should reach the artist.

I surveyed and interviewed visitors before designing

An investigative survey showed that our visitors would mostly be in their 20s to 40s, with a preference for simpler interfaces. We also interviewed local Japanese visitors and employees familiar with the artist to shape the product's language. This led us to a more cordial, polite tone for instructions, along with English guidance for visitors from abroad.

Solution

With the final Message Wall, visitors draw or write a message on their own phones and submit it to the LED screen near the exit. Their drawings are celebrated on the screen for everyone to see, saved to their phones, and then shared with the artist after the exhibition.

Product architecture

  2. Step 1DrawA visitor scans the QR code and draws on their own phone.
  3. Step 2SendThe drawing goes to the exhibition's server.
  4. Step 3MESSAGE WALLShow on the LED screenThe screen by the exit draws it in, line by line.
  5. Step 4Save to the phoneThe visitor keeps a copy with the exhibition logo.
  6. Step 5Archive for the artistEvery drawing is kept for the artist to see after the exhibition.

Key product decisions

Two decisions came from our research before launch. Testing with 50 users, including on-site crew and Japanese locals across varied technical backgrounds, led to three more.

From research

1. A branded save feature

Visitors had already shown how much they valued souvenirs and sharing their visit online. Saving each drawing with the exhibition branding made it a digital souvenir, and every shared drawing became organic promotion for the exhibition.

2. An artist archive

Visitors were told their messages would be sent to and seen by G-Dragon himself. Saving every submission for him to view personally turned a one-way fan experience into something reciprocal.

Displayed are samples of real submissions sent over the course of the exhibition.

From testing

3. Purposeful delay

We slowed down the drawing animations on the wall, so visitors had time to anticipate, prepare, and film their drawings appearing on the screen to share with others.

MESSAGE WALL

4. Icon placement and styling

Japanese testers preferred icons that were very clear to read, so every action felt intuitive at a glance. Much of the final icon placement and styling was decided based on their feedback on preferring clear, simple icons.

5. Mobile-first fixes

Much of the testing during development had been done on computer screens. Testing on phones revealed bugs and transition issues that came with scaling, so we made sure the doodle interface adapted to all devices for a consistent experience.

Outcome

3.1K+
Social media engagements related to the Message Wall

Visitors saved and shared their branded drawings online, extending the exhibition's reach beyond the venue. Each shared drawing promoted the exhibition in visitors' own words.

15%
Revisit rate from Tokyo exhibition visitors

Every drawing was archived for G-Dragon and his agency, so visitors' messages could reach the artist after the exhibition ended. This contributed to the revisit rate, as visitors wanted to be part of this new connection with the artist himself.

2K
Visitors per hour, on average

The LED screen gathered crowds near the exit, with visitors watching and celebrating each new drawing as it appeared.

Reflection

When I first started thinking about what to do with an empty LED screen, I didn't imagine it would become a place where visitors celebrated their own creativity and shared it with each other.

The most memorable part of designing, building and launching the Message Wall was the joy it brought. Every day on-site, I watched visitors cheer as their drawings appeared, point out each other's work, and film the screen to share online.

It taught me how much reliability matters. When an interface simply works, people stop noticing it and get to enjoy the moment it creates.
